Chapter overview

Tamil social history can be read through the language of communities, family, settlements, land, institutions, trade, religion and migration. This updated chapter follows those social structures from ancient Tamilakam to the global Tamil diaspora.

CommunitiesInstitutionsMigrationDiaspora
Scope, Sources and Historical Phases

Tamil social history follows communities, institutions, work, family, religion and migration across prehistoric, Early Historic, medieval, colonial and modern phases. Different source types reveal different parts of this long development.

Scope of the Chapter

The history of Tamil society covers the evolution of Tamil-speaking communities from prehistoric settlement to the modern Tamil diaspora.

This chapter concentrates on:

  • Social geography of ancient Tamilakam
  • Occupational and community terms
  • Family and marriage terminology
  • Position of women
  • Medieval land and settlement categories
  • Village institutions
  • Merchant organisations
  • Religious and linguistic communities
  • Historical migrations
  • Colonial-era social transformation
  • Expansion of Tamils outside Tamil Nadu

Detailed archaeology, Sangam political history, Tamil literature, freedom movements, the Justice Party, rationalism, Self-Respect and Dravidian movements are covered separately in later chapters.

Sources for Tamil Social History
Archaeological Sources

Stone tools, pottery, burials, habitations, coins, inscriptions, industrial remains and botanical evidence reveal material life.

Detailed archaeological sites and scientific dates are covered in Chapter 2.

Literary Sources

Important literary sources include:

  • Tolkappiyam
  • Ettuthokai
  • Pattuppattu
  • Pathinenkilkanakku
  • Silappadikaram
  • Manimekalai
  • Bhakti literature
  • Medieval commentaries
Epigraphic Sources

Inscriptions provide information on:

  • Personal and occupational names
  • Donations
  • Land categories
  • Village institutions
  • Merchant organisations
  • Religious establishments
  • Taxes and professional groups

Tamil Nadu has Tamil-Brahmi, Vatteluttu, Tamil, Grantha and Nagari inscriptions.

Colonial and Modern Sources

Government proceedings, district manuals, census reports, missionary records, newspapers and Madras Presidency documents are preserved in the Tamil Nadu Archives.

Chronological Framework
Prehistoric Phase
  • Palaeolithic hunting and gathering communities
  • Mesolithic microlith-using communities
  • Neolithic agricultural and pastoral settlements
  • Iron Age–Megalithic communities
Early Historic Phase
  • Growth of agriculture, crafts, writing, towns and ports
  • Sangam-era Chera, Chola and Pandya society
  • Tamil-Brahmi literacy
  • Inland and overseas trade
Early Medieval Phase
  • Pallava and Pandya agrarian expansion
  • Growth of Bhakti traditions
  • Rise of temple-centred settlements
  • Expansion of Brahmadeya villages
Imperial Chola and Later Pandya Phase
  • Large-scale irrigation and agriculture
  • Strong village institutions
  • Temple endowments
  • Merchant guilds and overseas commerce
Vijayanagara–Nayak Phase
  • Military and administrative migration
  • Expansion of Telugu-speaking communities
  • Saurashtra settlement
  • Growth of Palaiyams
  • Valangai–Idangai divisions
Colonial Phase
  • Madras Presidency administration
  • New land-revenue arrangements
  • Missionary education and printing
  • Census-based social classification
  • Urban and industrial growth
  • Overseas labour migration
Modern Phase
  • Expansion of public education
  • Urbanisation and industrial employment
  • Global Tamil migration
  • Growth of language-based identity
Ancient Tamilakam and Social Geography

Ancient Tamilakam extended from Vengadam to Kumari. The five landscapes connected environment with named communities, occupations, products and settlement patterns.

Ancient Tamilakam

Ancient Tamilakam broadly extended:

  • From Vengadam in the north
  • To Kumari in the south
  • Between the eastern and western seas

It included most of present-day Tamil Nadu and Kerala, with adjoining regions forming frontier zones.

The major cultural regions were organised through the Ainthinai, or five landscapes.

Five Landscapes and Communities
Kurinji

Region: Mountains and hill slopes

People: Kuravar Occupations: Hunting, honey collection and millet cultivation

Settlement term: Sirukudi

Mullai

Region: Forest and pastoral tract

People: Ayar and Idaiyar Occupations: Cattle, sheep and goat rearing

Main products: Milk, curd, butter and ghee

Marutham

Region: Fertile agricultural plains

People: Uzhavar and Vellalar Occupation: Settled agriculture

Main crops: Paddy and sugarcane

Neithal

Region: Coast

People: Parathavar

Occupations: Fishing, salt production, pearl diving and navigation

Palai

Region: Dry and difficult tract

People: Eyinar and Maravar in literary classification

Activities: Hunting, cattle raids, warfare and long-distance travel

The Thinai system connected landscape, community, livelihood, settlement and literary convention.

Sangam Social Groups and Performers

Sangam sources used specific terms for rulers, cultivators, pastoralists, merchants, bards and performers. These terms reveal social functions without representing one fixed modern caste system.

Important Sangam-Age Social Terms
Political and Elite Groups
  • Arasar — rulers
  • Vendar — crowned kings
  • Velir — minor chiefs
  • Kizhar — local chiefs or leading landholders
  • Anthanar — learned and ritual specialists
Productive Communities
  • Uzhavar — cultivators
  • Vellalar — agricultural and landholding communities
  • Ayar / Idaiyar — pastoralists
  • Kuravar — hill communities
  • Parathavar — fishing and maritime communities
  • Vanigar — merchants
Performers and Bards
  • Panar — singers, generally associated with the Yazh
  • Viraliyar — women performers
  • Koothar — actors and dancers
  • Porunar — bards associated with war and praise poetry

Tolkappiyam and Sangam literature refer to Panar, Koothar and Viraliyar as recognised performers within Tamil society.

Family, Marriage and Women

Early Tamil literature preserves a detailed vocabulary for courtship, marriage, friendship and reconciliation. Women appear as poets, workers, vendors, performers and advisers.

Family and Marriage Terminology
Kalavu

Kalavu referred to love and courtship before public or family recognition.

Karpu

Karpu referred to recognised married life and marital fidelity.

Arathodu Nittral

Arathodu Nittral was the process through which the heroine’s love was honourably disclosed to elders, generally through intermediaries.

Varaivu or Varaithal

Varaivu referred to the formalisation of marriage.

Oodal

Oodal referred to disagreement or a lovers’ quarrel.

Pangan and Pangi
  • Pangan — male friend of the hero
  • Pangi or Thozhi — female companion of the heroine

The Thozhi played an important role in courtship, communication, reconciliation and marriage negotiations.

Women in Early Tamil Society
  • Women poets named in Sangam literature include:
  • Avvaiyar
  • Okkur Masathiyar
  • Kakkaipadiniyar
  • Vellivithiyar
  • Nachellaiyar
  • Ponmudiyar
  • Allur Nanmullaiyar
  • Aathimandiyar
  • Women also appear as:
  • Viraliyar or performers
  • Agricultural workers
  • Pastoral workers
  • Salt producers
  • Vendors
  • Spinners and weavers
  • Avvaiyar was closely associated with Adiyaman Neduman Anji.
  • Okkur Masathiyar is known for poetry portraying a mother who sends her son to battle.
  • Kakkaipadiniyar Nachellaiyar is associated with poems preserved in Sangam anthologies.
  • Detailed literary contributions belong to Chapter 4.
Settlements, Markets and Early Religions

Settlement and market terms distinguished villages, ports and commercial spaces. Early religious life combined local worship, Vedic practices, Jainism and Buddhism.

Settlement Terminology
  • Sirur — small village
  • Perur — large village
  • Mudur — old or established settlement
  • Ur — village or settlement
  • Pattinam — commercial or coastal town
  • Puhar — harbour settlement
  • Nagaram — commercial town or merchant organisation in later usage

Settlement names often reflected size, age, occupation or commercial importance.

Market and Commercial Terms
  • Nalangadi — daytime market
  • Allangadi — evening or night market
  • Vanigar — merchant
  • Sungam — customs duty or toll
  • Angadi — market street or market

Pattinappalai and Maduraikanchi describe specialised markets, warehouses, foreign merchants and commercial streets.

Full details of Sangam trade and ports belong to Chapter 3.

Early Religious Communities

Early Tamil society contained several overlapping religious traditions:

  • Murugan worship
  • Mayon or Thirumal worship
  • Korravai worship
  • Hero-stone worship
  • Vedic sacrificial traditions
  • Jainism
  • Buddhism

Tamil-Brahmi cave inscriptions at Mangulam and other sites record stone beds and donations to Jain ascetics.

The Mangulam inscriptions mention:

  • A Pandya ruler named Nedunchezhiyan
  • Officials or workers associated with him
  • Jain monks
  • A mercantile group from Vellarai

They are assigned to approximately the third century BCE by the Tamil Nadu Department of Archaeology.

Temple-Centred Society and Land Categories

From the Pallava period, temples became major social and economic institutions. Land grants connected cultivation, revenue, religion, education and social authority.

Transition to Temple-Centred Society

From the Pallava period onwards:

  • Saiva and Vaishnava Bhakti expanded.
  • Temples became major landholders.
  • Temple settlements attracted artisans and service communities.
  • Music, dance and festivals became institutionalised.
  • Inscriptions recorded salaries, donations and occupational duties.

Temple personnel included:

  • Priests
  • Accountants
  • Musicians
  • Dancers
  • Watchmen
  • Gardeners
  • Cooks
  • Lamp lighters
  • Artisans

Tamil inscriptions record the employment and support of musicians and dancers by temples.

Medieval Land Categories
Vellanvagai

Land associated mainly with ordinary cultivators and non-Brahmin landholders.

Brahmadeya

Land or an entire village granted to Brahmins.

Devadana

Land or revenue assigned to a Hindu temple or deity.

Pallichchandam

Land assigned to Jain or Buddhist institutions.

Salabhoga

Land or income assigned for educational, charitable or feeding institutions.

These grants transferred land revenue and administrative rights to religious or educational bodies.

Village Institutions and Kudavolai

Medieval local administration operated through village assemblies and specialised committees. Uttaramerur provides detailed evidence for the restricted Kudavolai selection procedure.

Medieval Village Institutions
Ur

General village assembly.

Sabha or Mahasabha

Assembly associated especially with Brahmadeya villages.

Nagaram

Body associated with merchants and commercial settlements.

Nadu

A territorial grouping containing several settlements.

Variyam

A specialised committee responsible for a particular administrative function.

Important committees mentioned in Chola records included bodies concerned with:

  • Gardens
  • Tanks
  • Revenue
  • Gold testing
  • Annual administration
Uttaramerur and Kudavolai

The Uttaramerur inscriptions describe the selection of members to village committees through the Kudavolai procedure.

Names of eligible candidates were written on palm-leaf slips and placed in a pot for selection.

Eligibility conditions included:

  • Age qualifications
  • Property requirements
  • Tax payment
  • Educational or administrative competence

Disqualifications included:

  • Failure to submit accounts
  • Certain offences
  • Recent committee membership in specified circumstances

Kudavolai represents an organised system of restricted local selection. It was not universal adult democracy.

Merchant Guilds and Social Divisions

Merchant organisations linked Tamil regions with India and overseas markets. Valangai and Idangai divisions structured occupational precedence and sometimes produced conflict.

Medieval Merchant Organisations
Ainnurruvar

Also known as Disai Ayirattu Ainnurruvar, meaning the Five Hundred of the Thousand Directions.

Nanadesi

Merchants who operated across several countries or regions.

Manigramam

An important merchant organisation found in inland and coastal centres.

Anjuvannam

A commercial group generally associated with West Asian and Muslim maritime merchants.

Valanjiyar

Travelling merchants operating through regional networks.

Tamil inscriptions also mention groups such as Nagarathar, Ayiravar and Chitramezhi Periyanadu.

Merchant guilds maintained links with:

  • Sri Lanka
  • Southeast Asia
  • Western Asia
  • Other regions of the Indian subcontinent
Valangai and Idangai
  • Medieval and early modern occupational communities were grouped into:
  • Valangai — Right-hand division
  • Idangai — Left-hand division
  • The exact number and identity of communities in each division differed across time and place.
  • Disputes concerned:
  • Processional order
  • Temple honours
  • Flags and symbols
  • Use of streets
  • Market rights
  • Social precedence
  • Valangai–Idangai conflicts continued into the colonial period and sometimes resulted in violence.
Women and Temple Institutions

Medieval inscriptions record women as donors, patrons, performers, religious personnel and workers. Their status and functions varied greatly by period and institution.

  • Medieval inscriptions refer to women as:
  • Land donors
  • Temple patrons
  • Musicians
  • Dancers
  • Religious personnel
  • Agricultural workers
  • Important royal women included:
Sembiyan Mahadevi

A major Chola patron associated with temple renovation and bronze images.

Kundavai Pirattiyar

A Chola princess associated with religious and charitable endowments.

Temple Women

Women attached to temples were described through terms that varied by period and inscription.

They could receive:

  • Land
  • Produce
  • Salaries
  • Training in music and dance

The later devadasi institution developed through major social and economic changes and should not be projected unchanged onto every earlier inscriptional reference.

Vijayanagara–Nayak Changes and Saurashtras

Vijayanagara and Nayak rule encouraged military, occupational and linguistic migration. Saurashtra silk weavers became an important part of Tamil urban and textile society.

Vijayanagara–Nayak Social Changes

The Nayak kingdoms developed at:

  • Madurai
  • Thanjavur
  • Gingee

Major social changes included:

  • Growth of the Palaiyakkarar system
  • Settlement of Telugu-speaking military and occupational communities
  • Expansion of temple towns
  • Growth of Valangai–Idangai organisation
  • New court and festival traditions

Tamil Virtual Academy records migration into Tamil Nadu during the Nayak period by communities including Kammavars, Reddiars, Nayaks, Devangas, Komatis and Saliyars.

Saurashtra Community

Saurashtras migrated into Tamil Nadu and became particularly associated with:

  • Madurai
  • Silk weaving
  • Textile production

They were popularly known as Pattunoolkarar, meaning silk-thread workers.

Tamil Virtual Academy connects substantial Saurashtra settlement in Tamil Nadu with the Nayak period.

Muslim and Christian Tamil Communities

Muslim maritime communities and Christian missionaries contributed to trade, language, printing, education and literary culture while remaining part of Tamil-speaking society.

Muslim Communities

Tamil Muslim communities developed strongly in maritime and commercial centres.

Important centres included:

  • Kayalpattinam
  • Kilakkarai
  • Nagore
  • Nagapattinam
  • Porto Novo or Parangipettai
  • Pulicat
  • Periyapattinam

Important Tamil Muslim community terms include:

  • Marakkayar
  • Labbai
  • Rowther
Marakkayars

Particularly associated with maritime trade and shipping.

Rowthers

Traditionally associated in several regions with horses and inland commerce.

Labbais

Associated with Tamil-speaking Muslim religious and commercial communities.

Tamil Muslim writers produced distinct forms of Tamil Islamic literature while remaining part of Tamil linguistic society.

Christian Communities and Printing

European missionaries contributed to:

  • Tamil printing
  • Prose writing
  • Dictionaries
  • Grammar
  • Translation
  • Schools
  • Periodicals

Christian missionary publications played an important role in the growth of modern Tamil prose and print culture.

Important personalities included:

  • Henrique Henriques
  • Robert de Nobili
  • Veeramamunivar
  • G. U. Pope
  • Robert Caldwell

Their literary and linguistic contributions belong mainly to Chapters 6 and 7.

Colonial Transformation and Tamil Migration

Colonial rule reshaped revenue, classification, education, cities and employment. Labour recruitment carried Tamil communities across the Indian Ocean and beyond.

Colonial Social Transformation

Major colonial-era changes included:

  • Integration into the Madras Presidency
  • Monetisation of land revenue
  • Expansion of the Ryotwari system
  • Growth of Madras city
  • Missionary and government education
  • Census classification of castes and communities
  • Railways and labour mobility
  • Plantation migration
  • New professions in law, medicine, education and administration

Colonial censuses often converted fluid local identities into fixed administrative categories.

Print, education and employment encouraged the formation of caste associations, linguistic associations and modern political organisations.

Detailed socio-political movements are reserved for Chapters 20–29.

Tamil Migration under Colonial Rule

Tamil workers were recruited for plantations, railways, docks and construction projects in:

  • Sri Lanka
  • Malaya
  • Singapore
  • Burma
  • Mauritius
  • South Africa
  • Fiji
  • Réunion

Tamil Virtual Academy records that 16 families were sent from Tamil regions to the Sri Lankan highlands in 1824, marking an early stage of organised plantation migration.

Recruitment systems included:

  • Indentured labour
  • Kangani recruitment
  • Contract labour

Migrants created:

  • Temples
  • Churches and mosques
  • Tamil schools
  • Newspapers
  • Mutual-aid organisations
  • Cultural associations
Global Tamil Society and Rapid Revision

Global Tamil society emerged through ancient commerce, colonial labour migration and modern professional or conflict-driven movement. Rapid revision links the chapter’s key terms and associations.

Global Tamil Society

Modern Tamil communities are established across:

  • Sri Lanka
  • Malaysia
  • Singapore
  • Gulf countries
  • South Africa
  • Mauritius
  • Europe
  • North America
  • Australia
  • New Zealand

The Government of Tamil Nadu’s Tamizhar Thadam initiative documents Tamil migration history, global institutions and diaspora contributions.

The Tamil diaspora developed through three broad streams:

  • Ancient and medieval commercial movement
  • Colonial labour migration
  • Modern professional, educational and conflict-driven migration
Rapid Revision
Social Geography
  • Kurinji — Kuravar — hunting and honey collection
  • Mullai — Ayar — cattle rearing
  • Marutham — Uzhavar and Vellalar — agriculture
  • Neithal — Parathavar — fishing and pearl diving
  • Palai — Eyinar and Maravar — warfare and travel
Performers
  • Panar — singers and Yazh players
  • Viraliyar — women performers
  • Koothar — actors and dancers
  • Porunar — war and praise bards
Marriage Terms
  • Kalavu — premarital love
  • Karpu — recognised married life
  • Arathodu Nittral — disclosure of love to elders
  • Varaivu — formalisation of marriage
  • Oodal — lovers’ quarrel
Settlement Terms
  • Sirur — small village
  • Perur — large village
  • Mudur — old settlement
  • Pattinam — commercial or coastal town
  • Puhar — harbour settlement
Land Categories
  • Vellanvagai — cultivator-associated land
  • Brahmadeya — Brahmin land grant
  • Devadana — temple land grant
  • Pallichchandam — Jain or Buddhist institutional land
  • Salabhoga — educational or charitable endowment
Local Institutions
  • Ur — general village assembly
  • Sabha — Brahmadeya assembly
  • Nagaram — merchant or commercial body
  • Variyam — administrative committee
  • Kudavolai — committee-selection procedure
Merchant Organisations
  • Ainnurruvar — Five Hundred guild
  • Nanadesi — merchants of many countries
  • Manigramam — major merchant organisation
  • Anjuvannam — West Asian or Muslim maritime merchants
  • Valanjiyar — travelling merchants
Social Divisions
  • Valangai — Right-hand division
  • Idangai — Left-hand division
Historical Communities
  • Saurashtras — silk weavers; Pattunoolkarar
  • Marakkayars — maritime Muslim merchants
  • Rowthers — associated with horses and inland commerce
  • Labbais — Tamil-speaking Muslim community
Key Personalities
  • Avvaiyar — Sangam woman poet associated with Adiyaman
  • Sembiyan Mahadevi — Chola temple patron
  • Kundavai Pirattiyar — Chola princess and donor
  • Robert de Nobili — missionary associated with Tamil prose
  • Veeramamunivar — Tamil Christian writer and lexicographer
  • Robert Caldwell — comparative Dravidian linguistics
Core TNPSC Facts
  • Tamilakam extended from Vengadam to Kumari.
  • Tamil society developed through prehistoric, Early Historic, medieval, colonial and global phases.
  • Tamil-Brahmi records personal names, rulers, merchants and religious donations.
  • Mangulam inscriptions mention Pandya Nedunchezhiyan and Jain ascetics.
  • Bhakti contributed to the growth of temple-centred society.
  • Medieval temples functioned as major employers and landholding institutions.
  • Uttaramerur inscriptions describe the Kudavolai procedure.
  • Brahmadeya, Devadana and Pallichchandam were distinct land-grant categories.
  • Ainnurruvar, Nanadesi, Manigramam and Anjuvannam were important merchant organisations.
  • Valangai and Idangai were Right-hand and Left-hand social divisions.
  • Saurashtras became associated with silk weaving and were called Pattunoolkarar.
  • Christian missionaries contributed to printing, prose, education, grammar and dictionaries.
  • Colonial labour migration created Tamil communities across Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia, Africa and the Indian Ocean islands.
  • Tamil society today extends far beyond the political boundaries of Tamil Nadu.
